prize_parts.citation: for credible empirical analysis of how technology and international trade reshape labour demand, job polarisation and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B025 (Kiyotaki and Moore) to B037 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The change rests on one point: the composite-discovery worry I raised against B037 in round 1 is weaker for the Dorn trio than for the Katz variant. Autor, Dorn and Hanson wrote the import-competition papers. Autor and Dorn also wrote the job-polarisation paper on the growth of low-skill service jobs, which supplies the task-based account of labour demand. The trio therefore covers both the technology side and the trade side through its own joint work. It does not need the skill-premium race between education and technology, which is the strand that overlaps with Goldin's recognised work and with my own research on capital-skill complementarity. The one discovery is how technology and trade shocks reallocate labour demand across tasks, occupations and places, shown with transparent designs. The evidence has been replicated in other countries and datasets, the debated magnitudes are the kind of dispute that follows a mature programme, and the lesson about concentrated and persistent adjustment costs is general. Judged on originality, breadth, durability and attribution, I now rank it above B025. It is a prize for evidence that has been tested repeatedly, while the quantitative amplification in B025 depends heavily on calibration. I do not rely on the count of colleagues who prefer B037 as evidence of its merit. Several members raised the same evidentiary concern about B025 that I flagged myself, and I weigh those as arguments.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the Dorn trio leaves out Katz, whose skill-premium work is foundational for how economists think about the race between education and technology. The citation must therefore not claim the whole task or skill-premium literature. Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane also sit behind the task framework, and the 2023 and 2024 prizes are adjacent on technology, skills and inequality. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects and the robustness of shift-share designs are still contested. Preferring this trio also depends on treating the import-shock and polarisation papers as one body of work, which a colleague could reasonably reject. B025 and B001 keep a cleaner two-name attribution, and B025 is the more specific mechanism, so I do not think the choice is lopsided. I also have a field-proximity bias in both directions: toward macro-finance (B025) and, through capital-skill complementarity, toward the skill-premium literature.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B037 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz, and accepts that dropping Dorn is a cost. She says that if colleagues judge the two strands separable, the cleaner trio is the trade-shock one, and that the committee should decide this on attribution grounds.
responses.response: I take her at her word and argue the attribution case for Dorn. Autor-Dorn-Hanson is the trade-shock core. Autor and Dorn also have a joint paper on job polarisation, so the technology and task side is credited through authors already in the trio, not only through Autor. That answers the one-or-two-discoveries question for me: the trio's own papers contain both halves. Katz is the better name only if the committee wants the prize to honour the long-run skill-premium framework. That claim is where the overlap with Goldin and the omission of Acemoglu are most costly. I would word the citation around labour demand, polarisation and local adjustment, and claim nothing about the skill-premium history.

responses.point: Hassler (chair) moved from B004 to B037 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He prefers Dorn to Katz because of overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. He concedes that this drops the education-versus-technology framing, and he keeps the citation to empirical analysis of adjustment, not settled welfare conclusions.
responses.response: I agree with his reasoning on both counts. The incremental contribution of the Dorn trio, beyond recognised ground, is design-based evidence on how trade and technology shocks move workers across occupations and regions. I also accept his cost: the education-technology race is left to a different prize, or to Katz in a different configuration. Where I would add to his case is that Autor-Dorn on polarisation gives the technology half a home inside this trio, so the narrow wording does not leave technology unattributed. I share his caution that persistence of the effects is debated, and the citation should say 'analysis of adjustment' without asserting magnitudes.

responses.point: Dreber declined to include B025 for lack of credible, direct evidence on the collateral channel beyond the post-crisis narrative. She prefers Autor, Dorn and Hanson for B037 and stresses design credibility and replication.
responses.response: Her question about B025 is fair, and I could only partly answer it. From my recollection, there is firm-level evidence that real-estate price shocks move corporate investment through collateral values (Chaney, Sraer and Thesmar), and Japanese land-price studies and household-leverage evidence point the same way. I have not re-verified these sources. That evidence supports the direction of the channel but not the quantitative amplification, and amplification is what the 1997 model is known for. I concede the point on magnitudes, and it is part of why I have moved. Her standard of tests that hold up is the standard I now apply, and on it B037 does better than B025. I agree with her trio for B037.

responses.point: Enflo prefers Autor, Hanson and Katz because it spans the skill-premium and task framework and the trade-shock evidence. She calls Dorn in place of Katz a defensible variant that she has not resolved, and would move to Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee decides the prize should honour only the trade-shock design.
responses.response: Her conditional is the one I would like the committee to test. I do not think the Dorn trio is limited to the trade-shock design, because the Autor-Dorn polarisation work gives it a task-based technology component. If that holds, her condition for moving is met without narrowing the prize to the China shock. If colleagues instead think the education-technology framework is the main discovery, Katz is needed, and I would then want to hear how the claim is separated from the 2023 recognition. I do not think the composite problem disqualifies B037 for either variant, and Enflo and I agree on that.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the Autor-Dorn polarisation work and the import-shock papers are one discovery, which is the premise for treating the Dorn trio as coherent. If it judges them separable, I would return to a single clean mechanism (B025 or B001).
Whether leaving out Katz and the skill-premium framework undercredits the technology side, and whether the committee wants a prize that honours that framework.
How large and persistent the China-shock effects were, and how robust shift-share identification and task measures are.
Whether adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes should reduce the weight of B037, and whether the 2022 prize adjacency weighs against B025.
My recollection of the collateral-channel and polarisation literatures is from memory and has not been verified against sources.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson appears in my supplied profile. I disclose co-authorship with committee members Boppart and Hassler, neither of whom is a candidate. My research on capital-skill complementarity is adjacent to the skill-premium strand of B037, and I chose the Dorn trio partly for that reason, to stay away from the strand closest to my own work. I also work in macroeconomics, close to the macro-finance field of B025, which I now list only as an alternative. These are disclosures only and are not adjudicated.
